# St. Peter Dome
**The dome of St. Peter's** rises to a total height of 136.57 metres (448.1 ft) from the floor of the basilica to the top of the external cross. It is the tallest dome in the world.
Its **internal diameter is 41.47 metres **(136.1 ft), slightly smaller than two of the three other huge domes that preceded it, those of the Pantheon of Ancient Rome, 43.3 metres (142 ft), and Florence Cathedral of the Early Renaissance, 44 metres (144 ft). It has a greater diameter by approximately 30 feet (9.1 m) than Constantinople's Hagia Sophia church, completed in 537. It was to the domes of the Pantheon and Florence duomo that the architects of St. Peter's looked for solutions as to how to go about building what was conceived, from the outset, as the greatest dome of Christendom.

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Peter%27s_Basilica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Peter%27s_Basilica)


In his 1743 survey, Giovanni Poleni identified **16 main vertical cracks** (meridian cracks) distributed symmetrically along the circumference of St. Peter's dome.
Since the dome is divided into 16 sections (bounded by Michelangelo's ribs), the average geometric angle between one main vertical crack and the next is **22.5 degrees** (calculated by dividing the 360° of the total circumference by 16).

**Damage Geometry and Poleni's Calculation**
- *Section division*: The vertical fissures opened exactly in the middle of each of the 16 fields between the ribs, where the masonry was thinner and subject to hoop tension forces.
- *Independent arch model*: This precise geometric interval allowed Poleni to apply Hooke's law regarding arch statics. He no longer viewed the dome as a single continuous shell, but as 16 independent arches placed side by side, each 22.5° wide at the base.
- *Structural stability*: By proving that the line of thrust (the path of gravitational forces) still remained within the thickness of each individual "arch/section," Poleni demonstrated that the dome was not at risk of an immediate collapse by overturning. It simply needed to be banded to stop those specific angles from widening.

## About this example
Poleni's own plate of 1748 for the dome of St Peter's, traced into **83
voussoirs in five groups** - the lower dome, the two shells of the upper dome,
the rib between them, and the lantern.

*What it exercises.* The **dome** mode. A lune of a dome is not a slice of a
barrel: its width grows with distance from the axis, so the weight of each
voussoir is computed by **Pappus' theorem**, exactly, from the area and the
centroid the model already carries. The slice angle is Poleni's own 22.5
degrees, one sixteenth of the dome, taken from his survey of the sixteen
meridian cracks. The groups are a mechanical statement and not a label: the rib
is 3.8 m wide out of plane against 16.3 m for the shells, so it weighs what a
rib weighs. The lantern enters as two applied loads at the crown.

*Also here.* The three-dimensional view, where the lune is drawn as a solid with
the parallels of the dome dashed around it; and Hooke's cable, the hanging chain
whose inversion is the line of thrust - which is the analogy this very plate
introduced.

*Try.* Turn the dome mode off and watch the thrust line move. That difference is
Poleni's whole argument, and it is one checkbox.
